statement: Multiple sources converge on Samuel Ajayi Crowther's A Vocabulary of the Yoruba Language (1842/1843) as an early — possibly the first — instance of English-language missionary lexicography rendering Èṣù as "Satan"/"devil." This is significant because Crowther was himself Yorùbá (a freed slave who became the first African Anglican bishop), meaning the mistranslation was propagated through native-speaker Christian scholarship under missionary institutional pressure, not purely imposed from outside. Subsequent 19th-20th century dictionaries followed this precedent. In Yorùbá cosmology, Èṣù functions as messenger/intermediary between Olódùmarè and both the other Òrìṣà and humanity, delivering sacrifices/prayers, and as an enforcer of divine law — morally neutral, not evil.

sources.citation: Crowther, Samuel Ajayi. A Vocabulary of the Yoruba Language. London, 1843 (expanded ed. with Owen Vidal, 1852).
sources.author: Samuel Ajayi Crowther

notes: This specific citation is repeated across several converging secondary sources (Guardian Nigeria, OkayAfrica, alamojayoruba.com) but none is a peer-reviewed academic citation independently verified page-by-page against the primary 1843/1852 text — flagged as needing a firmer check before treating as fully settled at HIGH confidence.
